title: MA9-11438
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: INTRODUCTION [1] The following are the reasons for the decision concerning the claim of Mr. XXXXXXXX XXXXX (the Claimant), who is claiming under sections 961 and 97(1)2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the IRPA)3.

Claimant alleges that his cousin, XXXXXXXX, was a university student, in XXXXX, was arrested in XXXXX 2002, along with friends, and was detained and tortured as police accused them of helping militants. Claimant alleges that, in XXXXX 2003, his cousin was again detained for three days and tortured and police alleged that he was associating with militants.

Claimant alleges that the police raided his family home, on XXXXXX, 2003, because they were looking for his cousin. Claimant alleges that he was detained for two days and beaten during this time and questioned about the whereabouts of militants and his cousin.

Claimant alleges that the police did not stop harassing his family, as such, his father decided to send them out of India. The Claimant was able, with the help of an agent, to relocate to Kuwait and was able to work for different contractors. In XXXX of 2005, the Claimant returned to India to visit his family for approximately two months. However, police would have raided his home after his departure.

In XXXX of 2007, the Claimant returned to India as his contract in Kuwait was finished. Claimant alleges that on XXXXX, 2007, police arrested him and alleged that he had information about militants, including his cousin.
Claimant alleges that he was tortured and beaten while he was in custody, fingerprinted and photos were taken of him.

Fearing for his life, the Claimant was able to make arrangements to come to Canada on a work-permit. He left India on XXXXX, 2008. Claimant was laid-off by his Canadian employer. As such, fearing to return to India, the Claimant sought refugee protection inland, on August 8, 2009. Identity
The identity of the Claimant has been established to the satisfaction of the Panel, based on the photocopy of his Indian passport4.
The main issue to be determined in this case is internal flight alternative and the overall credibility of the Claimant.

Claimant testified that he decided that he had to leave India in XXXXX 2004, because of the problems that he had with the Indian police based in Punjab. He was first arrested in XXXXX 2003, because of his cousin. Asked where his cousin was presently, Claimant answered he did not know. Asked when was the last time he heard anything regarding his cousin directly or indirectly, the Claimant answered in XXXXX of 2003. When asked why the police was after his cousin, Claimant did not really have an answer, other than saying he took a religious course at school, however he was not a militant and Claimant stated that he did not have friends who were militants and did not really know why the police was after him.

The Claimant then testified that his cousin's mother still lives at the same house, at XXXX XXXXX, next to the house where the Claimant grew up and still speaks to his aunt. She says that the local police still frequently visit her asking for her son and for him. When asked if any of his cousin's siblings had any similar problems or visits by the police, the Claimant answered no because they live in other cities.

The Claimant was also asked if the police had visited his two brothers and four sisters who still live in India. The Claimant answered no. He also stated that one of his brothers and four sisters still live in XXXXX and one brother lives in XXXXX, which is 50 kilometres away. The Claimant is still in contact with his siblings form time to time. When asked if they have any particular problems in India, the claimant answered no. Asked if they ever had any problems with the police or anyone else, the Claimant answered no.

When pressed to give his opinion as to why the police would be on such a pursuit for his cousin whom the police allegedly accused of being a militant and also the Claimant to the extent of taking his fingerprints and torturing him, whereas they would not ever visit his brothers or his four sisters to find out his whereabouts and those of his cousin. The first time this question was asked, the Claimant did not really provide an answer, just simply said, his sister was married and there is no link, and, then, he said his brothers have left the family home about ten years ago. However, the Claimant was asked if the police wanted to trace them, then, why would they not look in these locations as possible hiding places for the Claimant and his cousin and, also, given the fact that their siblings would probably have some information as to their whereabouts. The Claimant stated again that it is probably because they moved away years ago and because of the fact that he was the closest in age to his cousin.

When asked about his wife and children and where they live presently, the Claimant answered: "About 120 kilometres away from XXXXXXXX". When asked if they had any problems since he left India, the Claimant answered that they have no problems since they moved because the police do not know where they live. When asked why the police from XXXXXXXX, would not have gone to visit his wife and children and his other siblings and family members, the Claimant answered because the police from XXXXXXXX would not go to other places. When asked if the police from different cities would not contact each other especially if there were people who were wanted, the Claimant answered that he does not think that local police would go in other jurisdictions or contact each other.

Then, during the hearing, there were some brief questions regarding the reavailment of the Claimant as he twice returned to India; the Panel, in its opinion, believes that the Claimant gave credible answers. The first time he returned is because his mother was ill and he wanted to see his mother before she passed away, which obviously is a reasonable reason why someone would take the risk to return. He also explained how, in 2007, he had to return because his work permit had expired in Kuwait and he could no longer remain there, which obviously is another reasonable explanation.

The Claimant did also provide reasonable explanations regarding his delay to claim in Canada because of the fact that he was here on a work permit and for him it was paramount to find a safe way into Canada regardless of status. The Panel is of the opinion, on a balance of probabilities, these are reasonable explanations.

However, the issues addressed beforehand, in the eyes of the Panel, open up a possibility of an internal flight alternative as it appears that the agent of persecution would not deploy any efforts to go see the Claimant's relatives which would be all located within a radius of about 120 kilometres. Furthermore, per the Claimant, his agent of persecution would not communicate with neighbouring police agencies to try to find the Claimant, which would corroborate findings found in the documentary evidence and confirmed in several decisions regarding the fact that many Sikhs who fear local police and who are of no interest to the central authorities can relocate to other parts of India5. This opinion is also corroborated in article 2.5 from the National Documentation Package6: "However, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services also noted that while the Punjab police may be serious about pursuing Sikhs anywhere in India whom they view as hard-core militants, in practice only a handful of militants are likely to be targeted for such long-arm law enforcement."

The Panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not demonstrate in any way that either himself or his cousin would be viewed as hardcore militants who would justify such attention. Notably, the Panel took in consideration the fact that the Claimant was able, as demonstrated by the stamps in his passport7, to re-enter India twice and leave three times, as evidenced in his passport. He was also able to obtain Canadian and Kuwaiti work-visas. By taking into consideration these aspects, the Panel is of the opinion that neither the Claimant nor his cousin would be perceived as hardcore militants, which, in the view of the Panel, would be the reason why the police would not bother looking for the Claimant or his cousin at their siblings' which lived at a very close distance.

Specifically, for possibilities of IFA, the cities of Bangalore, Mumbai or Rajasthan were suggested, where they would be opportunities for the Claimant considering his experience at different locations in Kuwait and in Canada and in Rajasthan where he has relatives.

The Claimant believes that he would still have problems in those locations at the hands of the police. For the reasons mentioned beforehand, the fact that the police has not gone to his siblings' looking for him and for his cousin, and since, as of XXXX 2010, when his wife and children moved 120 kilometres away, the police has not gone looking for the Claimant and his cousin at that location, and also, taking into account the fact that he was able to re-enter India on two occasions and was able to leave the country three times after his problems began as evidenced by the stamps in his passport, the Panel is of the opinion that there would be an internal flight alternative for the claimant at the suggested locations. Also, as mentioned before, he would not have the profile of a person whom the Indian police would deploy resources to find him at these locations. The Panel does not doubt that there could be some corrupt local police who would want to extort money from the Claimant or to harass him for various reasons. However, the Panel is of the opinion that the Claimant did not demonstrate that this could happen all across this large and very populous country.

Other factors which the Panel took into consideration regarding an IFA possibility for the Claimant was the fact that when he returned in 2005, for approximately three months, he did not have any problems during that time and that if he would have the profile of someone whom the Indian police would be after countrywide, the Panel is of the opinion that in this relatively small village, as described by the Claimant with XXXX votes8, that word would get around that the Claimant would be back in India for these three months. Also, the Panel took into consideration the fact that, in 2007, after he would have been released from prison, in XXXX, he moved to XXXXX to live there with his brother's relatives, and the Claimant was able to live there for approximately eleven months at this location without having any particular problems, although the Claimant said he did stay indoors for a good portion of this time there. However, the Panel is of the opinion that if the Indian police would be in pursuit of the Claimant all across India as he claimed, that, in these eleven months, they would have deployed resources to find him in XXXXX where he lived with his relatives..

The Claimant was also asked if other than his fear for his agent of persecution, if there was any other reason why it would be unreasonable for him to relocate to the three suggested locations, the Claimant gave no other reasons.
As shown, for all the aspects above-mentioned, the Panel is of the opinion that there would be an internal flight alternative for the Claimant in Bangalore, Mumbai or Rajasthan.

Despite the outcome of this hearing, the Panel wishes to state that it was not insensitive to the testimony of the Claimant which was very emotional, especially regarding the fact that he is an individual who just wants to give a better life to his family. The Panel could certainly appreciate these facts and also the difficulty the Claimant has had living most of the last seven years away from his wife and very young children. He has carried on his duties by supporting his family financially and also has gained international work experience in different fields. These are very commendable aspects; however, they unfortunately cannot be considered in such a claim. However, another forum which would have jurisdiction on these matters, could certainly consider these very important aspects.
The Panel concludes that the Claimant is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection".

As such, the claim of Mr. XXXXXXXXXXXX is rejected. Haig Basmajian Me Haig Basmajian September 16, 2011 Date /cl/ml REFUGEE PROTECTION DIVISION / POLITICAL OPINION / ARREST / DETENTION / TORTURE / RESETTLEMENT / REAVAILMENT / WORK PERMIT / INTERNAL FLIGHT ALTERNATIVE / MALE / NEGATIVE / INDIA 1 " 96. A Convention refugee is a person who, by reason of a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion, (a) is outside each of their countries of nationality and is unable or, by reasons of that fear, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of each of those countries; or (b) not having a country of nationality, is outside the country of their former habitual residence and is unable or, by reason of that fear, unwilling to return to that country." 2 " 97. (1) A person in need of protection is a person in Canada whose removal to their country or countries of nationality or, if they do not have a country of nationality, their country of former habitual residence, would subject them personally (a) to a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture; or (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if (i) the person is unable or, because of that risk, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of that country, (ii) the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country, (iii) the risk is not inherent or incidental to lawful sanctions, unless imposed in disregard of accepted international standards, and (iv) the risk is not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health or medical care." 3 S.C. (2001), chap. 27, as amended. 4 Exhibit A-2: Immigration documents, photocopy of Indian passport. 5 Singh, Balwant v. M.C.I. (F.C., no.
